title: Unrestricted Cypress task exposes arbitrary configuration values
description: The Cypress task `GetFromConfig` accepts an arbitrary configuration path from its caller and returns the corresponding value without an allowlist or sensitivity check. Any code running in the Cypress test/browser context that can invoke `cy.task` can therefore retrieve secrets or other internal configuration values from the Node process and receive them back into the test context. This is primarily a test-environment exposure, but it creates an unnecessary secret-exfiltration primitive if untrusted, injected, or compromised test code runs.

The supplied variable name is passed directly to the configuration provider with no allowlist, namespace restriction, or secret filtering.
The resulting configuration value is returned to the task caller, potentially exposing credentials, tokens, or other internal settings to the Cypress test context.

title: Unrestricted Cypress task exposes arbitrary configured memory fields
description: The `GetFromMemories` task also exposes an unrestricted property lookup over configured memory objects. A caller can choose any property name and receive the first truthy value, with no restriction to the intended challenge fields. If the configured memories contain sensitive or internal values, compromised or untrusted Cypress-side code can retrieve them through this task. The impact and reachability depend on the contents of the external configuration and the callers of the task.

title: Unrestricted address properties forwarded to create API
description: The service forwards the entire caller-supplied `params` object to the address API for creation without an explicit client-side allow-list. If the corresponding API handler performs automatic object binding, a caller can include server-managed address properties (for example ownership, user identifiers, verification flags, or internal metadata) and have them persisted. The frontend is not a security boundary, so this must also be enforced server-side; this finding identifies the unfiltered forwarding path and its reliance on backend controls that are not visible here.

The caller-controlled object is passed through unchanged as the POST request body; no explicit allow-list or property-level filtering is applied.
The unfiltered object reaches the address API create operation. If the server binds request properties directly to the address model, attacker-controlled sensitive properties can be persisted.

title: Unrestricted address properties forwarded to update API
description: The service forwards the entire caller-supplied `params` object to the address update API without an explicit allow-list. If the backend automatically binds request fields during update, callers may modify server-managed address properties such as ownership or internal status fields. The client cannot enforce authorization by itself, so the API must independently restrict updateable properties.

title: Unbounded chat request and response buffering enables resource exhaustion
description: `streamMessages` accepts an arbitrarily large message array and forwards it directly as the HTTP request body without any length, count, or content limit. It also subscribes to the streaming response immediately and appends every received chunk to an unbounded `chunks` array while waiting for the consumer. An attacker or abusive caller can submit very large prompts or cause a long-running/large model response, consuming client memory, network bandwidth, backend/model tokens, and potentially degrading service. No cancellation, maximum stream duration, response-size cap, or backpressure limit is enforced in this file.

trace.description: `streamMessages` receives the caller-supplied message array; the caller and any attacker-facing entrypoint are outside this file.
The supplied `messages` array is placed directly into the POST body, with no size or item-count validation before transmission to the chat endpoint.

The service stores every parsed response chunk in `chunks` and continues doing so until the stream ends, with no maximum buffer size, timeout, cancellation, or backpressure control. The loop later yields from that potentially unbounded buffer.

title: Path traversal in static data file loader
description: `loadStaticData` accepts an unconstrained `file` value and incorporates it into a filesystem path before resolving and reading it. A caller can supply traversal segments such as `../../outside/data/secret`, causing the resolved path to escape `./data/static/` and read any reachable file whose name ends in `.yml`. The contents are then returned after YAML parsing. The caller and attacker-facing route are outside this file, but the exported function provides the tainted entrypoint and contains no allow-list or containment check.

The caller-controlled `file` value is concatenated into a path and passed through `path.resolve`; traversal components can therefore escape the intended `./data/static/` directory. No basename validation, allow-list, or post-resolution containment check is performed.
The resolved path is opened with `readFile`, allowing access to files outside the static-data directory when a suitable `.yml` path is supplied.

title: Unbounded retrieval of all hints without pagination
description: `getAll()` retrieves the entire hints collection in one request and provides no pagination, result limit, or other client-side bound. If the backing `/api/Hints/` collection grows substantially, a caller that repeatedly invokes this service can cause the server and browser to process an unbounded response, consuming memory, bandwidth, and CPU and potentially degrading availability. The endpoint's public reachability and any infrastructure-level limits cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: Unbounded order-history retrieval without pagination

The caller and server-side route are outside this file, so the endpoint's reachability and existing infrastructure limits cannot be confirmed here.

title: Unbounded photo upload submitted to memories endpoint
description: The exported addMemory method accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied File and places it directly into a multipart request without enforcing a maximum file size, maximum upload count, or other client-side bound. A caller outside this file can invoke the method with a very large file, causing excessive browser memory/network use and potentially imposing substantial processing, storage, and bandwidth costs on the /rest/memories upload endpoint. Server-side limits may mitigate the issue, but no such control is visible here and client-side callers can also bypass this service and call the endpoint directly.

title: Unpaginated retrieval of the entire photo-wall collection
description: The get method requests the complete memories collection using a fixed collection URL and provides no pagination, limit, or cursor parameter. As the photo-wall dataset grows, a single unauthenticated or broadly reachable request can force the server to query and serialize all records and force the client to download and retain the entire response. Whether the backend applies an independent cap is not visible in this file.

title: Unbounded local backup parsing enables browser resource exhaustion
description: The restore API accepts an attacker-controlled File and reads its entire contents into memory, then parses the contents as JSON without any file-size or structural limit. A maliciously large backup file can cause substantial memory allocation and CPU consumption in the browser, potentially freezing or crashing the client. The same unbounded values are also later URL-encoded and submitted in parallel restore requests, increasing resource use.

title: Unvalidated backup contents control client state and progress restoration
description: The restore workflow treats a locally supplied JSON file as authoritative backup state. After checking only the numeric version, it writes arbitrary supplied values into client cookies and, when the user clicks the snackbar action, sends the supplied continue-code values to the server-side progress restoration endpoints. There is no schema validation, length bound, or verification that the codes originated from a genuine backup generated by this application. An attacker who can cause a victim to import a crafted backup can overwrite local progress state and cause restoration operations using attacker-chosen codes; the ultimate server-side authorization impact depends on validation in the called ChallengeService endpoints outside this file.

The only gate is backup.version === VERSION; arbitrary backup fields are then written to cookies, including continue codes, without type, length, provenance, or integrity validation.

After user confirmation, the untrusted continue-code values are URL-encoded and passed to restoreProgress, restoreProgressFindIt, and restoreProgressFixIt, which are external request sinks whose authorization and validation are not established in this file.

title: Unbounded recycle collection retrieval
description: The service exposes the recycle collection through `find` without enforcing pagination, a maximum page size, or any other response bound. The caller, which is outside this file, can invoke this method with arbitrary query parameters or omit them entirely; the request is then sent directly to the collection endpoint. If the backend returns the full collection (or honors an attacker-influenced large limit), a large recycle dataset can be materialized in the server response and browser memory, allowing repeated requests to consume bandwidth, server serialization resources, and client memory. The service itself contains no compensating bound, although backend pagination or infrastructure rate limiting cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: Unbounded conversation data causes synchronous storage exhaustion
description: Conversation persistence accepts an entire caller-supplied `StoredConversation` without any size, message-count, or content-length limit. The service reads all existing conversations, appends or replaces the supplied object, serializes the complete collection synchronously with `JSON.stringify`, and writes it synchronously to `localStorage`. An attacker or otherwise untrusted caller that can provide an oversized conversation or repeatedly add conversations can cause excessive serialization, sorting, memory use, and eventual localStorage quota failures. Because `save` does not catch quota or storage errors, subsequent conversation operations may fail and the client-side chat functionality can be disrupted.

The service loads the full existing conversation collection and either replaces one item or appends the caller-supplied object, allowing the in-memory collection and its serialized representation to grow without an application-level bound.

The entire unbounded collection is synchronously serialized and persisted to localStorage. Large input consumes CPU and memory, while repeated additions can exhaust the browser storage quota; no limit or exception handling is present.

title: Unrestricted payment-card payload forwarding enables property tampering
description: The service accepts an unconstrained `params` object from callers outside this file and forwards it wholesale to the Cards API. There is no explicit allow-list of client-controllable payment-card fields. If the API binds the request body directly to its card model, a caller can submit protected properties such as an owner/user identifier, internal status, or other model fields and have them persisted or acted upon. The server-side route and model binding are outside this file, so the impact depends on that API implementation, but this service provides no property-level restriction.

title: Unbounded product listing parameters permit excessive resource consumption
description: The product-listing method forwards an arbitrary parameter object to GET /api/Products without enforcing a maximum page size, result limit, or other bound. A caller outside this file can invoke `find` with parameters such as an extremely large `limit`/`pageSize` value, or omit pagination entirely, causing the backend to retrieve and serialize an unbounded product set. This can consume database, server memory, bandwidth, and browser memory, degrading availability. Any server-side pagination or rate limiting is not visible here and is not enforced by this client service.

The caller-controlled parameter object is passed directly to Angular HttpClient, which serializes its fields into the product-listing request without a maximum page size or result bound.
GET /api/Products is the resource-intensive listing sink. An attacker can request an unbounded or excessively large result set, consuming backend query/serialization resources and client memory.

title: Unsanitized feedback comment passed through Angular HTML security bypass
description: Feedback comments returned by the feedback service are incorporated into an HTML string and then explicitly marked as trusted with Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`. Because the comment is not sanitized or encoded before the bypass, an attacker who can submit or persist a feedback comment containing HTML/script-capable markup can have that markup rendered in the feedback gallery. This defeats Angular's normal sanitization and enables stored or reflected client-side XSS, depending on the feedback endpoint's persistence behavior.

Attacker-controlled markup such as an injected element with an event handler or other browser-executable payload can therefore execute in the user's browser.

title: Caller-controlled review author is submitted to the API
description: The service accepts an `author` value from its caller and forwards it directly as part of the review request. Because `author` is an identity-bearing property, a caller that can invoke this service can submit a review under another user's name unless the server independently derives and authorizes the author from the authenticated session. This file contains no allow-listing, identity binding, or other control preventing caller-selected authorship.

title: Caller-controlled basket ID is used for cross-basket reads and writes
description: The service accepts a caller-supplied basket identifier and uses it to read and mutate basket contents without performing any ownership or authorization check in this client-side flow. The caller is outside this file. An authenticated user can substitute another basket ID; if the backend does not independently enforce basket ownership, the service will read that basket and update existing items or create new items under it. The lookup error is also converted to an empty basket, after which creation requests still proceed, so a failed or unauthorized lookup does not stop the mutation attempt.

The supplied targetBasketId is passed directly to find(), which requests the corresponding basket resource.
Lookup failures are suppressed and replaced with an empty Products list, allowing the method to continue toward mutation rather than aborting on an unauthorized or invalid target.

Existing basket-item IDs from the target basket are used in PUT requests with no ownership check; the targetBasketId is also used for new item creation. If API-side authorization is absent or insufficient, substituting another user's basket ID enables unauthorized basket modification.
For products not found in the fetched basket, the caller-controlled targetBasketId is persisted into a new BasketItem request without a per-basket authorization check in this flow.

title: Unbounded guest basket merge creates concurrent API requests
description: Guest basket contents are attacker-modifiable client-side state, and this method imposes no maximum item count or maximum aggregate quantity before generating requests. Every distinct stored product creates a request, and forkJoin subscribes to all requests concurrently. A caller able to populate sessionStorage or invoke the public guest-basket methods repeatedly can cause an unbounded number of HTTP requests and large request payloads during merge, consuming browser and potentially API resources. The absence of a cap is visible here; infrastructure-level limits are not.

title: Test mock disables DomSanitizer security behavior
description: The test replaces Angular's DomSanitizer with a mock whose bypassSecurityTrustHtml implementation simply returns the supplied string unchanged. This disables the framework's security-trust behavior during component tests and means the suite does not exercise whether HTML passed to the feedback gallery is safely handled. Any unsafe feedback comment or markup-building regression could therefore remain undetected because the test accepts raw HTML as if it were trusted. The issue is confined to test coverage/configuration rather than directly deployed production behavior.

The test invokes the component's HTML-generation path and asserts that the value passed to the bypass API contains raw markup, but performs no sanitization or malicious-input assertion. Consequently, unsafe feedback content could pass this test without revealing a client-side output-handling regression.

title: Temporary 2FA authentication token exposed through localStorage
description: The 2FA verification flow retrieves the temporary authentication token from browser localStorage and submits it to the verification endpoint. localStorage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the origin and cannot be protected with HttpOnly or equivalent browser controls. Consequently, a same-origin script compromise can steal the temporary token and use it in the MFA verification flow, weakening the protection of the pre-authentication state. The file does not establish whether the token is additionally bound to a session, expires quickly, or is otherwise protected server-side.

The service reads the temporary authentication token from localStorage, where it is accessible to any same-origin JavaScript rather than being held in a browser-protected credential mechanism.

The retrieved temporary token and the caller-provided TOTP value are submitted to the 2FA verification endpoint; theft of the localStorage token can let a same-origin attacker interfere with or replay the MFA completion request, subject to server-side expiry and binding controls not visible here.

title: Bearer token forwarded to arbitrary request destinations
description: The interceptor adds the bearer token to every outgoing HttpRequest that reaches it, without restricting the destination origin. Because the caller controls the request URL and the interceptor does not distinguish same-origin API calls from absolute third-party URLs, any application flow that requests an external resource can transmit the user's session token to that external service. An attacker who can influence such a URL or induce a request to an attacker-controlled origin could capture the token and use it as the victim. This is also a security misconfiguration because credential forwarding lacks an origin allowlist.

The bearer token is placed on the outgoing request and passed to the next handler. Any external URL accepted by the caller therefore receives the session credential.

title: Client-controlled email identity asserted in authentication header
description: The interceptor copies the mutable browser-local value localStorage.email into an X-User-Email identity header on every request. Any script or client-side flow able to write localStorage can replace this value with another user's email, and the request carries that attacker-selected identity assertion to the server. If any backend authorization or user lookup trusts X-User-Email instead of deriving identity solely from a verified token/session, a user can impersonate another account or access that account's resources. The server-side trust relationship is outside this file, so exploitability is conditional but the client-side identity assertion is directly visible.

The interceptor reads email from localStorage, a client-writable store, without binding it to the verified bearer token or validating it against a trusted session identity.

The client-controlled value is emitted as X-User-Email on the outgoing request. If a server-side identity or authorization decision consumes this header, an attacker can substitute another user's email and perform actions as that user.

An authenticated user can manipulate the route to another user's address ID; the component then calls `getById` and, after editing, submits the same arbitrary ID to `put`. Whether exploitation succeeds depends on server-side authorization in `AddressService`/the API, which is outside this file, but this client workflow provides no per-resource authorization control and must not be treated as one.

On save, the same caller-selected identifier is passed directly to `AddressService.put`; there is no ownership or role check between route input and the mutation. An attacker can substitute another user's address ID and attempt to read or modify that address.

title: Checkout authentication gate trusts arbitrary localStorage token presence
description: The checkout flow treats the mere presence of a browser-controlled `localStorage` value named `token` as proof that the user is authenticated. The value is not parsed, signature-verified, checked for expiry, or validated with the server. An attacker can set `localStorage.token` to any value in their browser and navigate directly to `/address/select`, bypassing this client-side login gate. title: Unsigned JWT role claims control privileged route guards

title: Client authentication state trusts arbitrary localStorage token presence
description: The authentication helper is tested as logged in solely because an arbitrary string (`abc`) exists in localStorage under `token`. This demonstrates that the client-side identity decision does not validate token structure, signature, expiry, or server-backed authentication. An attacker able to write same-origin localStorage (for example through an XSS issue or compromised extension) can force the UI into an authenticated state and potentially access client-gated functionality. title: Unredacted progress-restoration errors exposed in browser logs
description: The component logs raw error objects from progress-restoration requests directly to the browser console. These errors originate from external service responses and may contain backend exception details, request metadata, or response payloads. Any user who can trigger a restoration failure can inspect the browser console and obtain unredacted diagnostic information, while the application has no visible sanitization, structured security logging, or control over sensitive fields included in the error object.

title: MFA-issued bearer token stored in script-readable storage without secure cookie attributes
description: After successful two-factor verification, the bearer authentication token is persisted in browser-controlled storage: `localStorage` and a JavaScript-set cookie. The cookie is configured only with an expiration time and no `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, or equivalent protection is supplied. Any script executing in the origin can read the localStorage token and the cookie value, and if the application is reachable over HTTP the cookie may also be transmitted without transport protection. Theft of this token allows an attacker to replay the authenticated session and bypass the MFA step until the token expires or is revoked.

title: No visible rate limiting or attempt lockout for MFA verification
description: The MFA verification operation can be invoked repeatedly without any attempt throttling, cooldown, or lockout in this component. Each invocation immediately calls `twoFactorAuthService.verify` with the submitted six-digit code, and the error path merely displays an error state for five seconds; it does not prevent additional requests. If the service/backend does not independently enforce rate limiting, an attacker can automate code guesses (up to 1,000,000 possibilities) and eventually obtain an authentication token through this MFA flow.

title: Client-controlled wallet amount passed into payment workflow
description: The wallet amount is taken from a client-side form control and written directly to `sessionStorage` without enforcing that the form is valid or deriving the amount from a trusted server-side state. If the payment workflow treats this value as the authoritative wallet funding amount, an attacker can alter the transaction amount and potentially obtain funds or credit without paying the intended amount. Server-side validation and recalculation are required; client-side validators alone are not an enforcement boundary.

title: Prerequisite tutorial can be bypassed with a fixed delay
description: The bonus challenge presents the DOM XSS payload without enforcing completion of the prerequisite DOM XSS tutorial. The hint is marked unskippable, but its resolution is only a fixed 10-second delay; the inline TODO confirms that no prerequisite-completion check exists. A user can therefore wait ten seconds and proceed directly to the bonus payload workflow, bypassing the intended learning sequence. title: Wallet address is used as an authenticated identity without signature proof
description: The component treats the wallet address returned by the injected provider as an authenticated identity and sends it to the backend without requesting or verifying a signed challenge. A wallet address is public and can be supplied directly by an attacker to the corresponding API, while this client-side connection step provides no server-verifiable proof that the caller controls the address. If the backend uses this value to associate the session, authorize minting, or perform other wallet-specific actions, an attacker can substitute another address and affect the identity used for authorization. The server must authenticate wallet ownership with a nonce-based signature verification flow rather than trusting the submitted address.

The backend-facing walletAddressSend operation receives the caller-selected address as the identity-bearing value; trusting this value for subsequent authorization enables identity substitution unless an external server-side signature verification control exists.

title: Remote Solidity compiler loaded without integrity verification
description: The component constructs a compiler URL for a remote Solidity compiler JavaScript bundle and passes it to `solidityCompiler` without any visible integrity verification such as a pinned hash, signature, or trusted bundled asset. If the remote artifact, DNS, CDN, or delivery path is compromised, the browser can load attacker-controlled compiler code in the application's origin. Because this component is also connected to `window.ethereum`, compromised compiler code could potentially access application data and attempt wallet-provider interactions in the user's browser.

title: Unbounded client-side Solidity compilation can exhaust browser resources
description: Compilation accepts arbitrary editor content and invokes a browser-side Solidity compiler without a source-size limit, compilation timeout, complexity limit, or cancellation mechanism. A caller can repeatedly submit very large or computationally expensive Solidity programs, or repeatedly trigger failing compilations whose errors are appended to `compilerErrors`, consuming browser CPU and memory and potentially freezing the tab. title: Frontend source discloses administrator credentials
description: The frontend challenge instruction embeds the administrator's email address and progressively reveals the administrator's password, ending at `admin123`. Because this file is part of the frontend, the values are exposed to any client who can inspect the shipped source or challenge data. The instructions explicitly direct the user to log in and state that the result is administrator authentication. If these are real or reused credentials, an attacker can authenticate as the administrator without discovering the password independently, resulting in administrative account takeover. Although this may be intentional for a training challenge, it is an unsafe configuration if the credential is valid in any deployed environment.

title: Plaintext login credentials embedded in client-side source
description: The exported frontend challenge instructions embed a live-looking email address and plaintext password directly in client-delivered source. The instructions explicitly guide a user to inspect the JavaScript bundle, recover these credentials, and authenticate with them. Any user able to load the frontend can retrieve the values through DevTools or static bundle inspection, enabling unauthorized login to the associated account and making the credentials effectively public. title: Client-controlled basket ID enables horizontal basket access
description: The basket resource identifier is intentionally exposed to and controlled by the browser through the `bid` session-storage value. The instruction explicitly directs a logged-in user to replace `bid` with another value, then confirms that the user is viewing another user's basket. This indicates that the downstream basket-loading flow trusts a client-controlled basket ID without enforcing ownership or authorization server-side. The actual lookup and authorization check occur outside this file, but this exported challenge instruction identifies the externally consumed client-controlled identifier and the resulting unauthorized resource access.

After the changed identifier is used by the application outside this file, the challenge declares success when the user is viewing another user's shopping basket. title: Raw bootstrap errors exposed through the production browser console
description: The application-wide bootstrap failure handler unconditionally writes the raw Error object to the browser console. Because this handler also runs in production, framework or initialization failures may expose stack traces, source paths, module names, and other internal diagnostic details to any user who can inspect the page's console. This weakens production diagnostic hygiene and provides attackers with implementation details useful for further attacks. The code also provides no controlled reporting or redaction path for these failures.

title: Unverified JWT role used as client-side admin authorization
description: The client-side admin-login wait gate treats an unverified JWT stored in localStorage as authoritative. The caller outside this file invokes waitForAdminLogIn(), which reads the token, decodes it without validating its signature or expiration, and accepts payload.data.role === 'admin' as proof of administrative identity. An attacker who can modify browser localStorage can place a forged token containing an admin role and cause this client-side gate to complete. This is exploitable wherever downstream client behavior relies on this helper as an admin authorization check; server-side authorization would be required to prevent the forged client state from granting real administrative access.

title: Solved challenge flags broadcast to every connected client

Because the event is sent to all connected clients rather than only to the user who legitimately solved the challenge (or an authorized audience), another connected user can receive flags for challenges solved by someone else and bypass the intended solve workflow. The caller and authentication context are outside this file, but the broadcast and inclusion of the flag are directly visible here.

Unless every caller independently supplies equivalent metadata, security events written through this logger cannot be reliably ordered or correlated across requests, weakening incident detection and forensic reconstruction. Because this code is shipped as client-side application code, users can inspect the bundle or source maps and recover a valid credential, then authenticate directly as Bender without exploiting the intended SQL injection challenge. Exposing a reusable password compromises the account and is both an authentication failure and a security misconfiguration.

The hook returns before examining changed fields, so a caller that performs an update with validation disabled can modify the supposedly non-updatable column. If this utility protects a role, privilege, verification, ownership, or other security-sensitive property, this permits unauthorized property modification.

The hook immediately returns when `options.validate` is false, without checking changed fields or rejecting updates. An update path that disables validation therefore reaches the model persistence operation without this constraint being enforced; the persistence operation is outside this file.

A protected property whose current value is null or undefined can therefore be set for the first time despite being declared non-updatable. This can enable unauthorized initialization of a security-sensitive property such as an administrative or verification flag, depending on how the helper is used.

If an attacker can influence application configuration (for example through a deployment/configuration injection path), this causes the server to make requests to attacker-selected destinations, including potentially internal services, and writes the response into the application's served frontend asset tree. The caller/configuration source is outside this file, but this function establishes the unsafe trust boundary and performs the fetch.

description: The startup restore routine enumerates every JSON file under a fixed directory and launches one asynchronous file copy per match through an unbounded `Promise.all`. There is no file-count limit, concurrency cap, or aggregate-size control. If an attacker or compromised component can populate `data/static/i18n` with a very large number of files, startup can consume excessive memory and filesystem/IO resources, potentially delaying or preventing application startup. The caller and the ability to write this directory are outside this file.

The value is passed directly to the dependency checker, which can cause the process to inspect an arbitrary directory/package manifest if an attacker can influence this argument. The same untrusted value is also written into warning and informational logs, potentially disclosing filesystem paths and allowing log-forging characters such as newlines to contaminate operational logs. The handler compares that value directly against the global notification `flag` and removes the matching notification without authenticating the socket, checking ownership, or otherwise authorizing the mutation. An attacker who learns or guesses a flag can suppress a notification for every connected client because `notifications` is shared process-wide.

description: The websocket connection handler sends every cached notification to each newly connected client, with no per-client authorization, pagination, or bound on the number of notifications emitted. If the shared notification cache grows large or an attacker repeatedly opens connections, the server performs unbounded iteration and emits the entire collection for each connection, creating avoidable CPU, bandwidth, and socket-output pressure. No application-level connection or event throttling is visible in this file.

title: Unbounded FTP PDF enumeration during startup cleanup
description: The startup cleanup enumerates every matching PDF in the FTP directory into an in-memory array without a count limit, timeout, or other resource bound. If an attacker or untrusted upload path can populate `ftp/` with a very large number of PDFs, one cleanup execution can consume substantial memory and perform a correspondingly large number of filesystem operations, potentially delaying or disrupting application startup. The caller and ability to populate this directory are outside this file.

title: OAuth authorized redirect URIs are unrestricted strings
description: The OAuth configuration accepts every string as an authorized redirect URI and does not require an HTTPS origin, restrict schemes, or constrain redirects to the application's own domain. If an attacker can influence a custom YAML/application configuration, they can configure an attacker-controlled redirect URI and cause OAuth authorization responses or codes to be sent to that URI, enabling account takeover or token theft. The schema is the validation boundary and provides no compensating restriction.

Negative or otherwise economically invalid prices are accepted, including deluxePrice, and the schema does not establish a non-negative or positive monetary invariant. If configuration can be influenced by an attacker or an untrusted configuration-import path, a product can be assigned a negative price and purchasing it may create a credit/refund imbalance or corrupt order totals. No compensating business-rule constraint is present in this schema.

If an attacker can influence the configuration, they can set the URL to an internal service such as a cloud metadata endpoint or localhost admin interface, causing server-side polling requests to reach it.

title: System-wide notification polling frequency is unbounded
description: The validation accepts any positive poll frequency, including arbitrarily small values, without a lower bound, maximum frequency, or rate limit. A caller that controls configuration can configure the notification poller to run at extremely high frequency, causing excessive timer activity and outbound requests and potentially exhausting CPU, connections, or the remote service. The actual polling loop is outside this file, but this file explicitly authorizes the unbounded value.

trace.description: The exported route factory receives an Express request from a caller outside this file; the attacker-facing route can supply the `file` path parameter.
The handler copies the attacker-controlled `params.file` value without canonicalization or a platform-independent traversal check.
The check rejects only `/`, not Windows `\\` separators or traversal segments such as `..\\..`; therefore a traversal payload can pass this validation on Windows.

The resulting path is resolved and served without verifying that the canonical path remains under `ftp/quarantine/`. On Windows, a payload such as `..\\..\\package.json` can resolve outside the quarantine directory and disclose an arbitrary readable file.

title: Payment card deletion lacks audit logging
description: The payment-method deletion workflow performs a security-relevant destructive action but emits no audit or security event in this file. A successful deletion can therefore occur without a record of which authenticated user deleted which card, impairing detection and investigation of account compromise or unauthorized payment-method changes. Centralized middleware logging may exist outside this file, but no route-local logging or explicit audit call is present.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported deletion handler for DELETE /api/Cards/:id; the route is protected by appendUserId middleware according to the supplied routing context.
The handler receives the target card identifier from req.params.id and uses the authenticated-user-associated req.body.UserId to scope the deletion.
CardModel.destroy performs the destructive payment-method deletion and returns success, but this security-relevant event is not written to an audit log or monitoring system in the handler.

title: Payment-method listing has no pagination or result limit
description: GET /api/Cards retrieves every payment card belonging to the current user with CardModel.findAll, but supplies no limit, pagination, or result cap. If a user can accumulate a large number of cards through other application paths, one request materializes and serializes the entire collection, allowing excessive database, memory, and response-processing consumption.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported payment-method listing handler for GET /api/Cards; the route is protected by appendUserId middleware according to the supplied routing context.
The handler queries CardModel.findAll scoped to req.body.UserId, but does not specify limit, offset, cursor, or another bound on the number of returned cards.
All retrieved cards are transformed and accumulated in displayableCards before the complete collection is serialized in the response, so a large per-user collection is processed in one request.

title: Unauthenticated access to arbitrary recycle records
description: The unauthenticated GET /api/Recycles/:id route accepts an attacker-controlled recycle record identifier and retrieves that record without checking the caller's identity or ownership. An attacker can substitute another user's ID and receive the matching recycle record, bypassing the separate list-blocking middleware. This is an unauthenticated BOLA/access-control failure; impact depends on the fields stored in the recycle record but can include unauthorized disclosure of another user's data.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the request from a caller outside this file for GET /api/Recycles/:id; the route is registered without authentication or authorization middleware.
The handler takes req.params.id directly from the request and parses it as the target record identifier. No authenticated user or ownership information is used to constrain the lookup.

RecycleModel.findAll queries by the caller-selected ID alone, and the resulting record is sent in the response without any per-record authorization check. User A can request User B's recycle ID and receive the matching record.

title: Unbounded unauthenticated profile image upload processing
description: The POST /profile/image/file route is reachable through upload middleware, but this handler does not enforce any file-size or upload-count limit before processing the attacker-supplied in-memory buffer. The buffer is passed to file-type parsing and then written to disk. An attacker can repeatedly submit very large files, causing memory consumption during upload and parsing, CPU consumption during type detection, and disk I/O/storage pressure. The route's external multer configuration may provide a limit, but no such control is visible in this file; additionally, authentication is checked only after the upload buffer has already been accepted and parsed, allowing unauthenticated callers to consume resources before rejection.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file registers this handler for POST /profile/image/file; the route has upload middleware but this handler itself receives and processes the resulting request file without a visible size limit.
The externally supplied file is read from req.file and its complete in-memory buffer is obtained before the authentication check at line 35.
The full attacker-controlled buffer is parsed to identify its type, consuming processing resources before the request is authenticated.

After parsing, the complete buffer is written to the server's upload directory. Repeated oversized uploads can consume memory, CPU, disk bandwidth, and storage; no size or rate control is enforced in this handler.

title: Unauthenticated restoration with forgeable hardcoded Hashids codes
description: The three restore-progress endpoints are reachable without authentication, yet they accept a caller-controlled continue code and mutate challenge state by solving every matching challenge. The code used to validate the continue code is not a secret: each route embeds its Hashids salt directly in source, and Hashids is an encoding/obfuscation mechanism rather than an authenticated token. An attacker can therefore reproduce the encoding and generate a valid code containing arbitrary challenge IDs, then invoke the endpoint to mark those challenges as solved without completing them or proving ownership of a progress state. The same defect exists in the FindIt and FixIt variants, which use separate but equally hardcoded salts.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported restoreProgress handler receives the attacker-controlled `params.continueCode`; the route caller and its lack of authentication middleware are outside this file.

The handler constructs Hashids with the hardcoded salt `this is my salt`. Anyone who can inspect the application or source can reproduce the code generation, and Hashids does not provide authenticity or integrity.
The attacker-controlled path parameter is decoded and accepted based only on its alphabet and whether decoding returns IDs; there is no signature, expiry, nonce, or user/progress ownership check.
Decoded IDs are compared against all globally loaded challenges, without restricting them to a progress record belonging to the caller.
For every matching arbitrary challenge ID, the server marks the challenge as solved, allowing a forged request to bypass the intended challenge-completion workflow and alter application state.

title: Unauthenticated checkout of arbitrary baskets
description: The exported checkout handler is registered for POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout without authentication middleware. It accepts an attacker-supplied basket ID, loads that basket without scoping the lookup to the authenticated customer, and then destroys its basket items and clears its coupon after generating an order. There is no ownership or authorization check between the lookup and mutation. User A can substitute User B's basket ID to check out or consume User B's basket, potentially causing unauthorized orders, inventory changes, and loss of the basket contents.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported placeOrder handler through POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout; the route is declared with no authentication middleware.
The handler takes the path parameter id directly from the request and uses it as the basket identifier.
The basket is fetched by id alone, with no authenticated-user ownership predicate or subsequent authorization check.

After processing, the handler clears the coupon and destroys all BasketItem records for the supplied basket ID, then returns an order confirmation. A caller who supplies another user's basket ID can therefore mutate and consume that basket.

title: Caller-controlled UserId enables arbitrary wallet debit and credit
description: The handler trusts req.body.UserId to select the wallet account involved in payment and bonus crediting. Because the route has no authentication middleware and the value is not derived from the authenticated session or checked against basket ownership, an attacker can supply another user's ID. With paymentId 'wallet', the code can decrement the selected user's wallet if it has sufficient funds; it also credits bonus points to the selected ID. This allows unauthorized financial operations against arbitrary wallet accounts.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout without authentication middleware.
The handler accepts UserId from the request body rather than resolving the target account from the authenticated identity.
The supplied UserId is used to look up a wallet and, when the caller selects wallet payment, to determine which account is charged.
The selected user's wallet is decremented and the same caller-selected UserId receives the earned bonus points; no ownership or authorization check constrains either operation.

title: Forged and indefinitely replayable client-side campaign coupons
description: The checkout accepts couponData supplied by the caller, merely base64-decodes it, and compares its embedded date to a hardcoded historical campaign date. Base64 provides no authenticity or integrity, and there is no expiration check relative to the current date or server-side issuance validation. An attacker can construct a value such as WMNSDY2019-<matching timestamp> and repeatedly obtain the historical 75% discount, reducing the order price without possessing a valid coupon.

trace.description: The checkout handler receives request-controlled order data and passes the request to calculateApplicableDiscount.
When the basket has no applicable server-side coupon, the function trusts req.body.couponData as the alternative coupon source.
The supplied value is only base64-decoded and split into a coupon code and caller-controlled timestamp; base64 does not authenticate the coupon contents.

A matching hardcoded campaign entry causes the embedded timestamp to grant the campaign discount, with no current-date expiration or signature/issuance validation. The resulting discount is applied to totalPrice.

title: Unauthenticated, unthrottled expensive checkout operation
description: POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout is exposed without authentication or any handler-local throttling, and each request performs database reads and mutations, dynamically imports and generates a PDF, writes a file, iterates over all basket products, and updates inventory. An attacker can repeatedly invoke the endpoint, including against baskets with many items, to consume database, CPU, filesystem, and connection resources. No rate limit, request quota, or other cost control is visible in this handler.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout with no authentication middleware, and the handler contains no rate-limit or quota enforcement.
The request causes a basket lookup and then performs per-product quantity reads and updates while constructing the order.
Each invocation dynamically loads PDFKit and creates a PDF backed by a filesystem write stream, with no local throttling or workload bound.

title: Unauthenticated notification replay enables notification spam
description: The unauthenticated `GET /rest/repeat-notification` endpoint accepts an attacker-controlled challenge name and invokes `sendNotification` whenever the named challenge is solved. Because the route has no authentication or authorization middleware and the solved state is not scoped to the caller, any unauthenticated party can repeatedly trigger notifications for globally solved challenges. Repeated requests can spam connected users and consume notification/event-processing resources. No per-user, per-IP, or per-endpoint throttling is visible in this handler.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file registers `repeatNotification()` for unauthenticated `GET /rest/repeat-notification`; the handler receives the external query object without an authenticated identity.
The attacker controls `query.challenge`, which is URL-decoded and used as the challenge selector. No caller identity, ownership, authorization, or request-rate check is performed.
The supplied name is resolved to a challenge and only its global `solved` flag is checked; there is no check that the requesting user is authorized to cause notifications for that challenge.

For any solved challenge, the handler calls `sendNotification` and returns success. An attacker can repeat requests to cause repeated notification delivery, potentially spamming users and consuming event/notification resources.

title: Unrestricted serving of encryption key files
description: The exported middleware accepts the caller-controlled `params.file` value and directly serves a file from the `encryptionkeys/` directory. It performs no authentication, authorization, or explicit allow-listing of which key files may be exposed. Any publicly reachable route using this handler can therefore disclose private or otherwise internal cryptographic key material by requesting its filename, potentially enabling decryption or token/signature forgery. The slash check only rejects forward slashes and does not establish that the requested file is safe; on Windows, backslash-based traversal or an absolute path can also escape the intended directory.

trace.description: `serveKeyFiles` returns an Express handler receiving request parameters from its caller; the route registration and any outer authentication middleware are outside this file.

The handler copies the attacker-controlled `params.file` path parameter and only checks whether it contains a forward slash. There is no per-file authorization, trusted-key allow-list, or validation that the requested resource is non-sensitive.
The weak check is applied before constructing the file path, but it does not protect key material generally and is bypassable for Windows backslash traversal or absolute-path input.
`res.sendFile` serves the resolved caller-selected path under `encryptionkeys/`, exposing any matching private/internal key file to whoever can invoke the route.

title: SQL injection in product search query
description: The unauthenticated product-search endpoint inserts the caller-controlled `q` query parameter directly into a raw SQL string. The 200-character truncation limits length but does not parameterize or safely constrain SQL metacharacters, so an attacker can submit crafted input such as a quote and SQL comment/operator syntax to alter the `WHERE` clause. This can expose deleted or otherwise unintended product data and potentially enable broader database impact depending on the database driver and permissions.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler is registered as the unauthenticated `GET /rest/products/search` route and receives the attacker-controlled request through `req`.
The handler reads `req.query.q` and only truncates it to 200 characters. No SQL-specific validation, escaping, or parameter binding is applied.

The untrusted `criteria` value is interpolated into a raw SQL statement passed to `models.sequelize.query`, including inside the `LIKE` predicates. The query is executed without replacements or bound parameters.

title: Unbounded unauthenticated product search results
description: The public search endpoint executes a full product-table query with leading-wildcard `LIKE` predicates and no `LIMIT`, pagination, or result-count cap. A request with a broad or empty search term can force the database to scan the table and return every non-deleted product, while the handler materializes and localizes every returned row before serializing it. Repeated unauthenticated requests can therefore consume database, application memory, CPU, and response bandwidth.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; this exported handler is reachable as unauthenticated `GET /rest/products/search`, allowing an attacker to invoke it repeatedly without an application-level identity or authorization gate.
The query term is capped at 200 characters, but there is no cap on the number of matching rows returned and no rate-limit or pagination logic in the handler.
The raw query uses leading-wildcard searches over `name` and `description` and has no `LIMIT`, so broad terms (including the empty term) can scan and return the entire non-deleted Products table.

title: Unrestricted brute force of password-reset security answers
description: The unauthenticated password-reset endpoint accepts unlimited security-answer guesses. The handler reads the caller-controlled email, answer, and replacement password, performs the security-answer comparison, and immediately updates the account when the comparison succeeds. No per-IP, per-account, or per-endpoint throttling, lockout, attempt counter, or equivalent control is present in this file. An attacker can repeatedly submit guesses for a target email until the security answer is recovered, then set a new password and take over the account.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/reset-password reaches the exported handler without authentication middleware; the caller and route registration are outside this file. The handler receives attacker-controlled request data through the Request body.
The handler accepts the target email, security answer, and new password directly from the request body.

The email is used to locate the security-answer record and the supplied answer is compared against the stored HMAC-derived answer. There is no attempt limit, rate limiter, lockout, or delay between guesses.

On a successful guess, the supplied new password is persisted for the located user, allowing the attacker to authenticate as that account. Repeated requests can drive unlimited authentication attempts and database/update work.

title: Password resets and failed recovery attempts are not audited
description: Password-reset attempts are security-relevant account-recovery events, but this handler contains no logging for failed answers, successful resets, or the resulting password change. An attacker can perform repeated takeover attempts without an application-level audit trail, reducing the ability to detect brute-force activity and investigate compromised accounts.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/reset-password enters this handler without authentication; the route registration is outside this file.
The handler processes the caller-supplied recovery identity and answer, but no security-event logger is invoked while validating the request.

Both the successful password mutation and the failed-answer response complete without recording the event, target account, source address, or outcome. The only use of the remote address is in an error message for missing input, not an audit log.

title: Authenticated users can perform unrestricted server-side requests via profile image URL
description: The POST /profile/image/url handler accepts `req.body.imageUrl` and passes it directly to `fetch()` without validating the scheme, hostname, port, resolved address, or redirect destination. Any authenticated user can make the server request attacker-selected URLs, including cloud metadata services, loopback services, or internal administrative endpoints. The fetched response is then written under the user's public profile-image path, providing a potential channel to retrieve internal response data.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the attacker-controlled HTTP request; its route registration is outside this file. The route is POST /profile/image/url and has no authentication middleware, although the handler later performs its own cookie-based authentication check.
The handler reads `req.body.imageUrl` directly as the destination URL. No origin, scheme, private-address, or redirect validation is applied.
The handler only checks whether the caller maps to any logged-in user; it does not restrict the destination or verify that the target is an approved image host.
`fetch(url)` causes the server to connect to the attacker-selected destination. Node fetch also follows redirects by default, so an initially permitted-looking URL can redirect to an internal target.

title: Unbounded remote response download enables resource exhaustion
description: The endpoint downloads an attacker-selected response and streams it directly to disk without a response-size limit, timeout, or rate/count control visible in this file. An authenticated attacker can point the URL at a very large or indefinitely slow response and repeatedly consume disk space, file descriptors, network connections, and request-handling capacity.

trace.description: The exported profile-image upload handler receives attacker-controlled input; the route caller is outside this file. The endpoint is POST /profile/image/url.
The request body supplies the remote URL, with no limit on the amount of data the server may retrieve from it.
The server performs the remote request without a timeout, maximum response size, or application-level throttling shown here.
The entire response body is converted to a stream and piped to a writable upload file. No byte counter, abort threshold, or content-length/body-size check limits disk consumption.

title: Unvalidated remote SVG content is stored as a public profile image
description: Remote content is trusted as an image based only on the URL's final extension. A malicious response from a URL ending in `.svg` is stored unchanged in the application's public images directory, and the user's profile is updated to reference that same-origin file. If the frontend renders profile images in a browser context that permits SVG content, attacker-controlled SVG markup can execute script or otherwise deliver stored XSS; the rendering sink is outside this file. More generally, the endpoint lacks content-type validation and sanitization for a publicly served uploaded file.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the attacker-controlled profile-image URL from the POST /profile/image/url request; the route caller and later browser rendering are outside this file.
The attacker controls `imageUrl`, which is used to select the stored file extension by taking the final URL component. This is not validation of the response's actual content type.
The response body from the attacker-selected URL is downloaded without MIME validation, image decoding, SVG sanitization, or content inspection.
The URL suffix can cause the destination filename to use `.svg`, while the untrusted response bytes are written unchanged into the publicly served uploads directory.

The downloaded public file is assigned as the user's profile image. A downstream profile-image renderer can therefore serve/render attacker-controlled SVG markup from the application's origin; that rendering sink is outside this file.

title: Attacker-controlled JavaScript injection in MongoDB $where query
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/products/:id/reviews handler accepts the path parameter and, when the noSqlCommandChallenge configuration is enabled, only truncates it before concatenating it into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. Truncation does not constrain the value to a numeric literal or otherwise neutralize JavaScript syntax. An attacker can submit an expression such as `1 || sleep(2000) || 1` or other JavaScript payloads, causing server-side code execution within the MongoDB query context and potentially altering which reviews are returned. This is exploitable without authentication because the route has no auth middleware. The attacker-controlled $where expression can also force expensive execution or invoke sleep-like behavior repeatedly, consuming database/worker resources and degrading availability.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file invokes the exported handler for unauthenticated GET /rest/products/:id/reviews, supplying the attacker-controlled `:id` path parameter through Express `req`.

The handler reads `req.params.id`; when the NoSQL command challenge is enabled it applies only `utils.trunc(..., 40)`, which limits length but does not validate that the value is a safe numeric literal or remove JavaScript operators and expressions.

The resulting value is interpolated directly into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression. MongoDB evaluates the assembled string as query code, so crafted input can inject additional JavaScript, change query semantics, or perform expensive/blocking computation. No parameterization or strict allow-list intervenes.

title: MongoDB `$where` JavaScript injection through order ID
description: The unauthenticated order-tracking handler embeds the caller-controlled `req.params.id` directly into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression. When the reflected-XSS challenge is enabled, the code only truncates the value and does not remove quotes or otherwise constrain JavaScript syntax. An attacker can submit an order ID containing a quote and JavaScript expression to alter the `$where` predicate, potentially matching arbitrary orders or executing attacker-controlled database-side JavaScript. The truncation limit does not prevent injection.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the attacker-controlled request and route parameter; the caller and route registration are outside this file. The route is GET `/rest/track-order/:id` and is registered without authentication.

The handler copies `req.params.id` into `id`. In the reflected-XSS challenge mode it applies only a 60-character truncation, which does not prevent quote characters or JavaScript operators from reaching the query expression.
The resulting value is interpolated into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression. Caller input can therefore change the expression's structure instead of being treated solely as data.

title: Unauthenticated access to arbitrary orders (BOLA)
description: The endpoint has no authentication or per-order authorization check and performs a lookup using the caller-supplied order identifier. Any unauthenticated requester who obtains or guesses another customer's order ID can receive that order's serialized record. The fallback response does not establish ownership, and there is no check between the lookup and the JSON response.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an external request; its caller and route registration are outside this file. Architecture registration exposes it as GET `/rest/track-order/:id` with no authentication middleware.
The target resource identifier is taken from `req.params.id` and used as the order lookup key. No authenticated identity or ownership context is consulted.
The database query searches orders by the caller-selected `orderId` without scoping the lookup to a user, session, or authorized account.
The query result is converted to JSON and returned directly to the requester, with no per-resource authorization check. User A can substitute User B's order ID and receive User B's order data.

title: Missing object-level authorization allows any authenticated user to edit another user's review
description: The authenticated user is read but never used to authorize the targeted review. The handler accepts a caller-controlled review identifier and updates the matching database record without checking that the caller owns the review, is its author, or otherwise has permission to modify it. User A can submit User B's review ID and replace its message, resulting in unauthorized cross-user modification.

trace.description: The exported route handler receives the request from the caller outside this file; the attacker supplies the target review ID and replacement message in the request body.
The handler obtains the authenticated user, but the resulting identity is not used in the database selector or any subsequent ownership check.
The caller-controlled req.body.id is used as the sole selector for the review update; no author, owner, role, or user-ID condition is added.
The database update persists req.body.message to the selected review, allowing an authenticated attacker to modify another user's review by substituting its identifier.

title: NoSQL operator injection enables bulk modification of product reviews
description: The request body field id is passed directly into a MongoDB query selector without enforcing that it is a scalar identifier. An attacker can submit an operator object such as {"$ne": null} instead of a review ID. This changes the query semantics from selecting one review to matching many reviews, while multi:true causes the attacker-controlled message to be written to every matching review. This is NoSQL/operator injection with a broad integrity impact.

trace.description: The exported handler receives attacker-controlled JSON in req.body from a caller outside this file.
The unvalidated req.body.id value, which may be an object rather than a scalar ID, is embedded directly as the value of the MongoDB _id selector.
The selector is executed by reviewsCollection.update without scalar-type validation or an allow-list preventing MongoDB operators; an input such as {"$ne": null} can match numerous reviews.
The update uses multi:true and writes the attacker-controlled message to every matched document, enabling bulk tampering with review data.

title: Stored XSS through unsanitized true-client-ip header
description: The unauthenticated route accepts the attacker-controlled `true-client-ip` request header and, when `httpHeaderXssChallenge` is enabled, deliberately skips `security.sanitizeSecure`. The raw value is persisted into the user's `lastLoginIp` field. If that field is later rendered in an HTML-capable administrative or user interface, an attacker can submit a payload such as an HTML/script-bearing header and achieve stored XSS. The rendering sink is outside this file; the vulnerability is introduced at the persistence point.

trace.description: `saveLoginIp()` is an exported handler factory invoked by the caller outside this file for the unauthenticated `GET /rest/saveLoginIp` route; the handler receives the attacker-controlled Express request at this point.

The handler reads the caller-supplied `true-client-ip` header. Because the route has no authentication middleware, an attacker can send an arbitrary header value after satisfying only the handler's later session check.
When `httpHeaderXssChallenge` is enabled, the empty branch leaves the header value unchanged; the sanitization call is only in the `else` branch.

The unsanitized attacker-controlled value is persisted as `lastLoginIp` through the user model update. Any later HTML rendering of this field, outside this file, can interpret the payload as markup or script.

title: Login IP can be spoofed through a client-controlled header
description: The handler treats the client-provided `true-client-ip` header as the user's login IP. A caller can set this value to any address or arbitrary string, and the fallback to the socket address is used only when the header is absent. Unless a trusted proxy strips and rewrites this header before the application receives it, users can falsify the recorded login IP, undermining audit data and any downstream IP-based security or abuse-detection decisions.

trace.description: `saveLoginIp()` is called for `GET /rest/saveLoginIp`; the route declaration indicates no authentication middleware, while the handler receives the external request from a caller outside this file.
The handler obtains `true-client-ip` directly from request headers, allowing the caller to choose the value presented to application logic.
The socket-derived address is used only if the header is undefined; supplying any header value therefore bypasses the server-observed IP fallback.
The selected value is written to the authenticated user's `lastLoginIp` field, creating forged login-origin data for downstream auditing or IP-based controls.

title: Hardcoded plaintext test credentials in source
description: A plaintext username and password for the Jim test account are committed directly in the test source. Anyone with access to the repository or generated source artifacts can obtain these credentials and attempt authentication against any environment where the fixture account exists and retains this password. This is particularly risky if test credentials are reused in shared, staging, or accidentally exposed deployments.

trace.description: The test runner invokes the asynchronous setup hook; the caller and repository access boundary are outside this file.
The setup authenticates as the fixed account before exercising the address API, causing the credential values below to be used for login.
A plaintext password is embedded in the source code as the login credential. The email is also hardcoded at line 23, allowing the complete credential pair to be recovered from the repository.

title: Administrative application configuration endpoint is expected to allow unauthenticated access
description: The test accesses the administrative application-configuration endpoint without supplying any authentication credentials and explicitly expects a successful 200 response. This indicates the admin configuration resource is reachable unauthenticated. If the endpoint returns deployment details, feature flags, paths, or other internal settings, an attacker can use it for reconnaissance and potentially obtain sensitive configuration data. The production route implementation is outside this file, but this test establishes the expected unauthenticated behavior.

trace.description: The test begins an administrative application-configuration access check; the caller-facing route implementation and authentication middleware are outside this file.
A SuperTest request is created directly against the application without an Authorization header, session, or other credential setup.
The request targets GET /rest/admin/application-configuration.
The test requires the unauthenticated request to succeed with HTTP 200, establishing that this administrative configuration endpoint is expected to be publicly accessible.

title: Hardcoded reusable passwords and TOTP secrets in authentication tests
description: The test source embeds reusable TOTP secrets and plaintext account passwords. For example, the TOTP secret at line 42 is used to generate a valid second-factor code for the seeded `wurstbrot` account, while the same account's password is embedded at lines 140-142. Multiple additional setup/disable test accounts use hardcoded passwords and TOTP secrets. Anyone with access to the repository or test artifacts can reproduce valid authentication factors for these accounts; if the fixtures or seeded accounts are reachable in a shared, staging, or misconfigured deployment, this enables unauthorized login or 2FA operations. Even if these are intended only as test fixtures, keeping reusable authentication secrets and passwords in source is an insecure configuration practice.

trace.description: The test suite is initialized by `createTestApp`; the application/test environment setup is outside this file, and the resulting app is then exercised by the requests below.
The test embeds a fixed TOTP secret and uses it to generate a valid one-time code for a fixed user ID (`userId: 10`).
The generated code and a signed temporary token are submitted to the 2FA verification endpoint, demonstrating that the hardcoded secret is directly used as an authentication factor.
The same fixture account is logged in using a plaintext hardcoded password and the same TOTP secret, making both reusable authentication credentials present in source.

title: Plaintext test account credential committed to source
description: The test embeds a plaintext password (`ncc-1701`) for the `jim` account in source code. If this repository or its test environment is accessible to an attacker, the credential can be reused to authenticate as that account. Although this appears to be a test fixture credential rather than a production secret, storing reusable credentials in source is an unsafe configuration practice and can become impactful if test credentials or environments are exposed or reused.

trace.description: The test receives the application instance from `createTestApp`; the application and seeded test users are provided by code outside this file.
The test invokes the login flow for the `jim` account using a password held directly in the test source.
A reusable plaintext password is present in the source and is supplied to the authentication request, allowing anyone with access to the source to attempt authentication as the test account.

title: Unauthenticated access to global Web3 listener state
description: The exported handler is registered as unauthenticated, yet any caller can invoke a state-changing operation that mutates process-wide state and initializes a WebSocket contract listener. The request-supplied wallet address is accepted without authenticating or authorizing the caller, so an attacker can register arbitrary addresses in the shared listener state and trigger listener creation. This permits unauthorized manipulation of application-wide behavior and may consume the configured Alchemy/WebSocket resource.

trace.description: Entrypoint: POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress is registered without authentication or authorization middleware; the caller is outside this file and reaches the exported handler returned by contractExploitListener().
The handler takes walletAddress directly from the external request body without verifying the caller's identity or authority over the address.
The attacker-controlled address is inserted into the process-wide walletsConnected Set, changing shared state used by the contract event callback.
The same unauthenticated request can initialize a process-wide WebSocketProvider and contract event listener, an operation that is not protected by any server-side authorization check.

title: Unbounded attacker-controlled growth of wallet address Set
description: Each request can add a new caller-controlled value to the process-wide walletsConnected Set, but this Set has no size bound, expiration, cleanup policy, or rate limiting. An attacker can repeatedly submit distinct walletAddress values, causing unbounded in-memory growth. The only removal occurs when a matching ContractExploited event is observed, which an attacker cannot rely on and which does not cap registrations. The retained Set is consulted by the long-lived contract event listener, and no bound or cleanup control protects the memory-consuming state; only an event-driven deletion is present for matching exploited addresses.

title: User-controlled username persisted without XSS protection
description: The unauthenticated POST /profile route reaches this handler, which accepts req.body.username and persists it directly to the authenticated user's record without sanitization or an explicit safe-character allow-list. If the username is later rendered in an HTML-capable context without appropriate output encoding, an attacker can store markup or script that executes in other users' browsers. The rendering sink is outside this file, but the persistence point introducing the stored injection is present here.

title: Profile update endpoint lacks visible rate limiting
description: The profile mutation performs a database lookup and update for every authenticated request, but this handler contains no per-user or per-endpoint throttling, request frequency control, or other abuse limit. An attacker with a valid account or token can repeatedly submit POST /profile requests to consume database and application resources. Deployment-level rate limiting may exist elsewhere, which cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: Successful profile identity changes are not audited
description: Changing a user's profile identity field is a security-relevant account event, but this handler does not emit an audit or security log for successful username changes. Consequently, repeated or unauthorized-looking profile mutations may not be reconstructable from application security logs. Logging or audit middleware outside this file could provide coverage, so the finding is limited to the absence of logging in this code path.

title: Client-controlled wallet increment permits arbitrary balance manipulation
description: The wallet top-up endpoint accepts `req.body.balance` directly as the amount used to mutate the persisted wallet balance. There is no server-side validation that the amount is positive, bounded, or corresponds to an authorized payment amount. A caller with a valid card can submit an arbitrarily large positive value to create wallet credit, or a negative value to decrease the balance. This allows direct manipulation of a sensitive wallet property and violates the intended payment/top-up business rule.
