title: User-controlled username reaches server-side eval
description: The authenticated user's stored username is treated as executable JavaScript when it matches the `#{...}` pattern and the challenge is enabled. An attacker who can create or modify a username containing such a payload can cause arbitrary JavaScript to execute inside the server process during profile rendering. The result is then inserted into the Pug template source and compiled, potentially enabling further server-side template injection. This is not merely output rendering: the explicit `eval` executes attacker-influenced code with the privileges of the application process.

title: Profile response CSP permits unsafe-eval
description: The response's Content-Security-Policy explicitly enables `unsafe-eval` for same-origin scripts. This weakens the browser-side CSP mitigation against XSS and permits same-origin JavaScript to invoke dynamic evaluation. In this handler, user-derived content is also incorporated into the generated profile HTML, so allowing `unsafe-eval` reduces defense in depth if a client-side injection reaches a script context. The policy should avoid `unsafe-eval` unless there is a documented, unavoidable requirement and an equivalent stronger control.

The handler constructs a CSP response header for the generated profile page.
The policy explicitly includes `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'`, disabling CSP's restriction on JavaScript dynamic evaluation for same-origin scripts.

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of users' security questions
description: The exported handler is reachable at GET /rest/user/security-question without authentication. It accepts an attacker-controlled email address, queries for the corresponding user's security answer record, then returns that user's security question. There is no authentication, ownership verification, or other authorization check tying the requested email to the caller. An attacker can submit another user's email and learn the account's security question, aiding targeted account-recovery attacks; the distinction between a returned question and an empty object also permits account enumeration.

The security question is returned to the unauthenticated caller. For nonexistent or unmatched emails, the handler instead returns an empty object, providing an additional account-existence signal.

title: Basket item can be reassigned to an arbitrary basket after creation without a basket ownership check
description: An authenticated caller can create a basket item without a BasketId and then assign it to an arbitrary basket identifier. The test explicitly expects POST without BasketId to succeed and subsequently expects PUT with BasketId 3 to return 200. This creates a potential basket-reassignment path that bypasses the apparent ownership validation applied when BasketId is supplied during creation (where BasketId 42 is rejected). If the target basket belongs to another user, this can move or inject items into another user's basket and potentially affect checkout state. The implementation of the route and ownership check is outside this file, so cross-user exploitability cannot be fully confirmed here.

title: Hardcoded Ethereum private key in test source
description: A raw Ethereum private key is hardcoded in the test source and submitted directly to the application. Anyone who can access the repository or distributed test artifacts can obtain this credential and potentially use it to authenticate to the challenge or control the associated wallet, depending on how the application uses the key. Test fixtures do not eliminate the risk when the value is a real or reused credential.

title: Unrecognized REST paths disclose Express and internal error details

title: Unauthenticated video streaming endpoint has no application-level throttling

title: Unbounded global CAPTCHA request tracking enables memory exhaustion
description: The CAPTCHA-bypass middleware records a timestamp in a process-global array using a monotonically increasing request counter, then increments that counter without any bound, expiration, or rate limit. Because the route is publicly reachable as POST /api/Feedbacks, an attacker can send repeated requests and force the array to grow indefinitely, consuming process memory and eventually degrading or terminating the service.

title: Unauthenticated callers can mark arbitrary challenges as solved

description: The application publicly exposes a directory listing for `/encryptionkeys`. An unauthenticated caller can enumerate files in a directory that contains cryptographic material, including the separately retrievable premium AES key. Directory indexing exposes internal security-sensitive resources and makes discovery of otherwise hidden files trivial.

trace.description: The test application is created by `createTestApp`, whose implementation is outside this file; the request below exercises the attacker-facing application without supplying authentication.
A request to `GET /encryptionkeys` is issued with no authorization or authentication material.
The response is expected to succeed with HTML content and contain an Express directory-listing title, confirming that directory indexing is enabled and publicly reachable.

title: Premium-content AES key is publicly downloadable
description: An unauthenticated request can retrieve `/encryptionkeys/premium.key`, which the test identifies as the Premium Content AES key and expects to receive with HTTP 200. Disclosure of the key allows anyone who can obtain the encrypted premium content to decrypt it, defeating the confidentiality control. The endpoint therefore exposes cryptographic material through a public file-serving route.

trace.description: The test application is initialized by `createTestApp`, defined outside this file; the subsequent request models an external caller accessing the file-serving route without authentication.
The caller requests `GET /encryptionkeys/premium.key` and supplies no credentials or authorization header.
The application is expected to return HTTP 200 for the premium AES key, demonstrating that the cryptographic key is exposed through the public endpoint.

title: Access logs are publicly exposed as downloadable files
description: The application serves an access-log file directly from a public URL and expects a successful binary response without authentication. Public access to server access logs can disclose request paths, timestamps, client metadata, and other operational or potentially sensitive information, while allowing attackers to inspect activity and reconstruct incidents.

trace.description: The application under test is created by `createTestApp`, outside this file; the following unauthenticated request exercises the public file-serving entrypoint.
A caller requests an access-log path under `/support/logs`, with the timestamped filename generated locally by `utils.toISO8601` rather than protected by an authorization check in this request.
The route is expected to return HTTP 200 with `application/octet-stream`, confirming that the access-log file is downloadable through the application.

title: Hardcoded privileged credentials in test source
description: The test source contains plaintext credentials for privileged accounts, including the administrator password `admin123` and the accountant password. These values are passed directly to the authentication helper and are therefore exposed to anyone with access to the repository or test artifacts. If the corresponding seeded accounts are reachable in a deployed environment, an attacker can authenticate as an administrator or accountant; even if intended only for tests, storing credentials in source is an insecure configuration practice.

trace.description: Test execution begins the authentication flow by calling the external `login` helper with a hardcoded administrator email and password; the caller/helper implementation is outside this file.
The administrator credential is propagated as an inline plaintext value, `admin123`, and analogous privileged credentials are supplied in the accountant tests.
The hardcoded credentials reach the authentication helper, which uses them to obtain bearer tokens for requests to privileged order-history endpoints.

title: Authenticated users can read another user's basket by changing the basket ID
description: The authenticated user represented by `authHeader` can request another user's basket by supplying its numeric identifier. The test logs in as Jim, then requests basket 2 using a bearer token and receives the basket object with HTTP 200. The resource lookup is therefore not scoped to the authenticated user, enabling BOLA and exposure of another user's basket contents.

trace.description: The test's caller is outside this file; the test establishes an authenticated session for `jim@juice-sh.op` and stores the resulting bearer token in `authHeader`.
The request accepts the caller-controlled basket identifier `2` in the URL while sending Jim's bearer token.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and a JSON basket whose ID is 2, demonstrating that the identifier lookup succeeds for a basket belonging to another user without an ownership check.

title: Checkout does not enforce ownership of the basket being finalized
description: The checkout workflow accepts basket 2 while using the global authenticated token created for Jim, then successfully places an order. Because the basket identifier is supplied by the caller and the operation returns an order confirmation, a user can potentially purchase or otherwise finalize another user's basket. This is a higher-impact instance of the same missing object-level authorization.

trace.description: The test's caller is outside this file; `authHeader` was initialized from the Jim login and remains the credential used for the checkout request.
The test applies a coupon to basket ID 2 using Jim's bearer token, showing that the workflow accepts a caller-selected basket identifier rather than deriving the basket from the authenticated user.
The same authenticated caller submits `POST /rest/basket/2/checkout` and receives a successful order confirmation, demonstrating that the foreign basket can be finalized.

title: Forged coupon grants a 99% discount
description: A caller can submit a coupon generated as a forged coupon with a 99% discount, and the application accepts it and applies the discount to basket 2. The test demonstrates a broken business rule for coupon authenticity/integrity: a discount token that is intended to be unforgeable can be manufactured and used to obtain an extreme price reduction. The implementation of `generateCoupon` is outside this file, so the precise cryptographic weakness cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: The test's caller is outside this file; the test constructs a coupon explicitly named `forgedCoupon` with a 99% discount value.
The forged coupon is URL-encoded and sent as the caller-controlled `coupon` path parameter for basket 2.
The endpoint responds successfully and reports `discount: 99`, proving that the forged discount is accepted rather than rejected as unauthenticated or invalid.

title: Hardcoded user and administrator credentials in source
description: The source contains hardcoded authentication credentials, including the administrator password `admin123` and fixed user passwords. If this test configuration or repository content is reused in a deployed/test-accessible environment, anyone who obtains the source can authenticate with these credentials; the administrator credential is especially dangerous because it can provide privileged access. The test-only context reduces certainty about production reachability but does not remove the hardcoded-secret misconfiguration.

The file hardcodes a normal user's password and later hardcodes the administrator account password `admin123` when obtaining an admin bearer token.
Those hardcoded credentials are passed to the login operation and used to create bearer tokens for authenticated API requests.

title: Plaintext reusable account password committed in payment API test
description: The test source contains a reusable plaintext account password (`ncc-1701`) passed to the login helper. Anyone with repository or test-artifact access can recover the credential and authenticate as `jim@juice-sh.op`; if this account exists in a shared, staging, or deployed test environment, the exposed credential can provide unauthorized API access. The impact is somewhat environment-dependent because this is a test fixture, but the plaintext credential is directly present in source.

The hardcoded password reaches the login operation, which exchanges it for an authenticated bearer token used by subsequent payment-card API requests.

title: Unauthenticated product modification due to missing function-level authorization
description: The PUT /api/Products/:id endpoint allows an unauthenticated caller to modify an existing product. This test invokes the route without an Authorization header, supplies a product identifier and attacker-controlled description, and receives HTTP 200 with the modified value. The route implementation is outside this file, but the test provides a direct proof that function-level authorization is missing for this mutation. Any unauthenticated attacker can tamper with arbitrary product records by changing the identifier.

trace.description: This test exercises the attacker-facing PUT /api/Products/:id route; the route handler and its authorization logic are outside this file.
The request targets the product identifier tamperingProductId and does not set an Authorization header. It sends an attacker-controlled description in the request body.
The application responds with HTTP 200 and the response contains the supplied description, demonstrating that the unauthenticated mutation succeeds.

title: Hardcoded user and administrator credentials in API test source
description: The test suite embeds multiple plaintext authentication credentials, including the administrator password `admin123` and several user passwords, directly in source. Anyone with access to the repository can recover these credentials and attempt authentication against any environment where the corresponding accounts exist or where test fixtures are exposed. The administrator credential is especially risky because it is used to obtain an authenticated token for subsequent API requests.

title: CAPTCHA answer disclosed to the client, allowing trivial bypass
description: The CAPTCHA endpoint response exposes the CAPTCHA answer in `captchaRes.body.answer`, and the test immediately submits that returned value to complete the data export. This means a caller can request a CAPTCHA and obtain its answer from the same JSON response, defeating the CAPTCHA's purpose as an anti-automation control. An authenticated attacker can therefore automate exports without solving the challenge.

trace.description: The test begins an authenticated data-export flow that is intended to require a CAPTCHA after the challenge is requested.
The authenticated caller requests `/rest/image-captcha` and receives a JSON response, whose body is asserted to be available to the caller.

The returned `answer` field is read from the CAPTCHA response and sent directly as the answer for the protected export request, demonstrating that the challenge can be solved without independently solving the CAPTCHA.

title: Internal error details exposed in data-export responses
description: The tests confirm that internal exception messages are returned in HTTP 500 responses. A mocked `MemoryModel.findAll` failure is returned verbatim as `Memory error`, while database failures expose contextual messages such as `Error retrieving orders` and `Error retrieving reviews`. If this behavior is reachable in a deployed environment, attackers can use induced errors to obtain implementation details and improve subsequent attacks. The producing route handler is outside this file, but the client-visible disclosure is explicitly asserted here.

The test replaces `MemoryModel.findAll` with a mock that throws an internal exception, creating a controlled server-side failure during export processing.

The response body is asserted to contain the internal exception text `Memory error`, proving that server-side error details are exposed to the caller. Parallel assertions at lines 352-353 and 367-368 confirm the same pattern for orders and reviews failures.

title: Data-erasure request leaves the user account active
description: The erasure workflow accepts an authenticated erasure request but does not remove or disable the account. The test submits an erasure request for the logged-in user and then successfully authenticates the same account, demonstrating that the supposedly destructive privacy operation has no effective deletion consequence. A user can therefore believe their data has been erased while the account remains usable and associated data remains available.

trace.description: The test invokes the attacker-facing POST /dataerasure/ endpoint with an authenticated user's token; the route implementation is outside this file.
The request carries the target user's email as form data, causing the erasure workflow to process that account.
After the erasure request returns successfully, the test logs in with the same credentials and receives HTTP 200, proving that the account was not deleted or disabled.
The successful authentication assertion confirms the business-rule failure: the erasure operation does not actually erase the user's account.

title: User-controlled layout path enables arbitrary local file disclosure
description: The POST /dataerasure/ workflow accepts a caller-controlled layout path and the test demonstrates that a path traversal value can read an existing application file. Supplying '../package.json' returns content containing the application's package metadata, while a nonexistent traversal path produces a filesystem error. This exposes internal files and also appears to disclose filesystem errors to the caller. The production route is outside this test file, but the request and resulting response establish the exploit behavior.

trace.description: The test invokes the attacker-facing authenticated POST /dataerasure/ endpoint; the route and file-reading implementation are outside this file.
The request supplies '../this/file/does/not/exist' as the layout value, demonstrating that the server accepts a caller-controlled filesystem path and exposes the resulting filesystem error.
The test then supplies '../package.json' as the layout path, reaching the server-side file-rendering operation.
The successful response contains 'juice-shop' and truncated file content, demonstrating disclosure of an internal application file to the requester.
The response-content assertions confirm that data from the requested local file is returned in the HTTP response.

title: Hardcoded reusable account credentials in test source
description: Source-controlled tests contain reusable plaintext account passwords, including a plaintext password for bjoern@owasp.org and another credential repeated in multiple authentication requests. If these fixtures correspond to accounts in a reachable test, staging, or accidentally deployed environment, anyone obtaining the repository can authenticate as those users. The values should be provisioned as isolated test secrets or generated dynamically rather than embedded in source.

The same source-controlled credential is used to obtain an authentication token and place it into a request cookie.
The credential is also embedded in a direct login request, making it a reusable authentication secret for the referenced account if that account exists in a reachable environment.
The password is transmitted as the login credential in the request body, confirming that the literal is an operational authentication secret rather than merely test data.

title: Plaintext account credentials embedded in test source

These values are passed directly to the login helper and may be reused by local, CI, or test deployments. If any corresponding accounts or seeded credentials are reachable outside an isolated test environment, repository readers or anyone with access to the deployed test instance can authenticate as those users, including the administrator. The code does not obtain these credentials from protected test secrets or environment configuration.

title: Unauthenticated access to recycle records
description: The test invokes GET /api/Recycles/1 without setting an Authorization header and expects a successful response containing recycle records. If this test reflects the deployed route behavior, an unauthenticated attacker can retrieve a recycle resource by supplying its identifier. The route also does not demonstrate any ownership check, so substituting another user's recycle ID could expose their data. This is an access-control failure; the test itself does not implement the route, so the production reachability and ownership behavior should be verified in the handler.

trace.description: The test directly exercises the attacker-facing GET /api/Recycles/:id endpoint; the production route handler is outside this file.
The test first creates a recycle record, but that setup request is authenticated only because it explicitly sets authHeader; the subsequent read request is separate.
The request targets recycle identifier 1 and does not set an Authorization header, allowing an unauthenticated caller to choose the object identifier.

The test expects HTTP 200 and consumes the returned data as an array of recycle records, demonstrating that the endpoint is intended to disclose the resource without authentication or a visible per-resource authorization check.

title: Feedback creation permits caller-controlled user impersonation
description: The feedback creation API accepts a caller-supplied `UserId` and persists it without enforcing that anonymous callers or authenticated callers may only create feedback for themselves. The test demonstrates both cases: an anonymous request creates feedback attributed to user 3, and an authenticated user submits a different user ID and receives a successful response with that association. An attacker can therefore create records in another user's name, causing impersonation and data-integrity problems.

trace.description: The test exercises the attacker-facing `POST /api/Feedbacks` endpoint; the server-side route and persistence implementation are outside this file.
The request body supplies `UserId: 3` directly while using only the public JSON header and CAPTCHA flow, showing that an unauthenticated caller controls the identity attached to the feedback.
The API returns HTTP 201 and the response record retains `UserId` 3, confirming that the caller-controlled identity is accepted and persisted.
A separate authenticated request also supplies an arbitrary `UserId: 3` rather than deriving the identity from the bearer token.
The authenticated request succeeds with HTTP 201 and returns the selected user ID, confirming the missing per-user authorization check on the persistence path.

title: Hardcoded plaintext account credential in source
description: A plaintext password for the account `bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com` is embedded in the test source and passed to the login helper. Anyone who can read the repository or its test artifacts can recover and attempt to use this credential against the test or another environment where the account/password is reused. This is especially risky if test credentials are not isolated from deployed credentials.

The account email is hardcoded in the test source, identifying the credentialed account.
The plaintext password is hardcoded and supplied to the login helper, exposing a reusable authentication secret in source control.

title: Profile image URL upload permits server-side requests to caller-controlled hosts
description: The profile-image URL upload endpoint accepts a caller-supplied URL that can target localhost. This test starts a local HTTP server and submits its address as `imageUrl`; the request succeeds with a redirect, demonstrating that the application processes/fetches a server-side URL selected by the caller. An attacker could substitute loopback, cloud metadata, or other private-network addresses to probe or retrieve internal resources, subject to the behavior of the handler outside this test file.

The test creates an HTTP service bound to a dynamically assigned local port, providing a reachable internal destination controlled by the test caller.

The caller supplies `http://localhost:${mockPort}/photo.jpg` as the `imageUrl` field. The application accepts and processes this caller-controlled internal URL, returning a successful redirect, which demonstrates the SSRF-capable URL-fetching path.

title: Security answer creation accepts caller-controlled UserId without ownership verification
description: The test demonstrates that an authenticated caller can create a security answer for a different user by supplying that user's identifier in the request body. A newly registered user is created at lines 56-64, but the subsequent POST uses the pre-existing `authHeader` rather than credentials associated with the new user, while sending `UserId: userRes.body.id` and expecting a successful 201 response. The endpoint therefore appears to trust the caller-controlled `UserId` without verifying that it belongs to the authenticated principal. An attacker could substitute another user's ID and set or influence that user's security-answer data, potentially undermining account-recovery controls.

trace.description: The caller, outside this test file, reaches the POST `/api/SecurityAnswers` endpoint using an authenticated request; this test invokes that attacker-facing entrypoint.
The request body selects the target account through the caller-controlled `UserId` field, using the ID returned for a separately registered user rather than an identity derived from `authHeader`.

The request is authenticated with the pre-existing `authHeader`, not with credentials for the newly registered user, demonstrating that authentication and target-user ownership are distinct in this flow.
The test expects HTTP 201, showing that the server accepts creation of a security answer for the supplied user ID without an ownership check visible in this execution path.

title: Empty product searches return an unbounded result set
description: The product search endpoint is explicitly tested to return the complete product collection when the caller supplies an empty `q` value. Because the request contains no pagination, maximum-result, or other bounding control, an attacker can repeatedly issue empty searches and force the server to retrieve, serialize, and transmit the entire catalog per request. The endpoint implementation and any infrastructure throttling are outside this file, so the finding is based on the unbounded behavior established by this test.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint exercised by the test: `GET /rest/products/search?q=` accepts an empty search term without any visible page size or result limit.

The test verifies that the response contains as many products as the complete `/api/Products` collection, demonstrating that an empty search causes the endpoint to enumerate the full catalog rather than return a bounded page.

title: Hardcoded plaintext test credentials
description: The test suite embeds a plaintext username and password (`jim@juice-sh.op` / `ncc-1701`) and uses them to obtain an authenticated session. If this account or credential is shared with a deployed test/staging instance, repository readers can replay the credentials to authenticate as that user. The code provides no indication that the credential is injected from a secret store or isolated from reachable environments.

The setup creates the test application and then invokes the login helper with a literal account email and plaintext password.
The hardcoded credentials are submitted to the authentication helper to obtain a session token, and the resulting token is placed into a Cookie header for subsequent authenticated requests.

title: Order tracking accepts injected identifiers and returns all orders
description: The test demonstrates that the order-tracking endpoint accepts an attacker-controlled expression in the `id` path parameter and returns a successful response containing the complete order collection. The payload at line 28 (`' || true || '`) bypasses the intended lookup for one order, while the assertions at lines 31-45 verify that multiple order records and their associated product data are returned. This permits unauthorized enumeration of order identifiers, customer email addresses, prices, and product details. Returning the entire collection also creates an avoidable resource-consumption risk if the order set grows large, because the endpoint has no observable pagination or result bound.

trace.description: The test issues a request to the attacker-facing order-tracking endpoint; the route implementation is outside this file, and this file supplies the attacker-controlled path value.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200 for the injected order identifier, showing that the malformed value is accepted rather than rejected as an invalid order ID.

The response is asserted to contain an array in `res.body.data`, and the test iterates through every returned order and its products, demonstrating that the injected identifier can produce a collection-wide result rather than a single authorized order. The unbounded collection response can disclose all matching records and consume memory and response bandwidth as the dataset grows.

title: Unauthenticated security-question lookup enables account enumeration and recovery-information disclosure
description: The unauthenticated security-question lookup accepts an arbitrary email address and returns the associated security question. The test demonstrates a distinct response for an existing account (the question is returned) versus an unknown account (an empty object), allowing remote account enumeration. More importantly, exposing a user's security-question prompt to anyone who knows or guesses the email discloses authentication-recovery information and can facilitate targeted security-question attacks. The endpoint's implementation is outside this file, but this test directly establishes the externally observable behavior.

The request supplies an attacker-chosen email address as the email query parameter.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and a concrete security-question object for an existing user's email address, exposing authentication-recovery metadata.

title: Unauthenticated malformed-input request leaks internal database error details
description: A request to the security-question endpoint without the required email parameter produces an HTTP 500 response containing an HTML error page with the application name and the underlying database/ORM error (`WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value`). This exposes internal implementation details to an unauthenticated caller and indicates that malformed public input is not converted into a controlled client error.

The request omits the required email query parameter, supplying malformed external input to the endpoint.
The endpoint responds with HTTP 500 and an HTML error page containing the application name and raw ORM/SQL-layer validation text, rather than a generic controlled client error.

description: The test source contains a hardcoded account email and password, with the password represented only as reversible Base64 encoding. These credentials are passed to the login helper and then used to obtain a bearer token. Anyone with access to the repository or test artifacts can decode and reuse the credential against the configured application or any environment where this account exists. The same credential pair is repeated at lines 107-109.

The hardcoded credential is sent to the login helper, which obtains an authenticated bearer token that is subsequently used for API access.

title: Wallet listener creation succeeds for invalid wallet addresses
description: The test demonstrates that the wallet event-listener workflow accepts an invalid caller-supplied wallet address and still reports successful listener creation. A caller can submit `walletAddress: 'lalalalala'`, receive HTTP 200 with `success: true`, and cause the server-side workflow to proceed without establishing that the address is valid. This permits creation of listeners for malformed or unintended targets and bypasses a required input invariant. The route implementation is outside this file, but this test directly exercises and confirms the insecure behavior.

The test treats the endpoint's successful response and `Event Listener Created` message as the expected result, confirming that invalid input reaches successful listener creation rather than being rejected.

title: Hardcoded administrative credentials in source code
description: The Cypress administration setup embeds a plaintext administrative login credential (`email: 'admin'`, `password: 'admin123'`) directly in source code. Anyone who can read the repository, test artifacts, or CI configuration can recover the credential and attempt to authenticate as the administrative account. If this account or password is shared with a deployed or non-isolated environment, this can result in administrative account compromise.

title: Weak redirect allow-list validation enables open redirect
description: The redirect endpoint accepts a destination because an allow-listed URL appears only inside the destination's query string. The test passes `/score-board?satisfyIndexOf=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop` and confirms that it is redirected and followed successfully. This demonstrates weak substring-style destination validation rather than parsing the URL and comparing its origin. An attacker can place an allowed URL in an attacker-controlled external URL's query, path, or userinfo and potentially cause victims to be sent to an arbitrary site.

The test explicitly supplies a destination where the supposedly allowed URL is merely embedded in the query string, rather than being the destination origin.
Following one redirect succeeds and returns the scoreboard page, confirming that the endpoint accepted and issued a redirect for the weakly validated destination.

title: Unhandled redirect errors expose internal exception details
description: Requests that omit the required redirect parameter trigger a 500 response containing the application name, the exception type `TypeError`, and implementation details such as `of undefined` and the failing `includes` operation. This exposes internal diagnostic information in an HTML response to an unauthenticated caller, helping attackers fingerprint the framework and infer server-side code and failure conditions. The companion test at lines 81-90 confirms the same behavior for an unrecognized query parameter.

title: Deterministic per-character RSA enables plaintext recovery
description: The script uses deterministic textbook RSA independently on each character and publishes the RSA modulus and exponent. These paths are cryptographic or challenge-related key material and are explicitly copied into the release artifact without redaction, exclusion, or environment-specific protection. Anyone who obtains the generated package can extract these files and potentially use them to decrypt protected data, forge tokens/signatures, or compromise security features that rely on the packaged keys.

trace.description: The `package` Grunt task is invoked by a caller outside this file; it runs the replacement, compression, and checksum steps.
The compression task defines the contents of the distributable archive and writes it under `dist/`.
The archive input explicitly includes the `ctf.key` file.
The archive input also explicitly includes every file under `encryptionkeys/**`, with no filtering or secret-management control.

title: Release integrity checks use collision-broken MD5
description: The packaging task generates MD5 checksum files for every artifact in `dist/`. MD5 is collision-broken and is unsuitable as an authenticity or tamper-detection mechanism: an attacker able to replace a package can construct a different file with the same MD5 under practical collision conditions. If consumers rely on these generated checksum files to validate release integrity, the check can be bypassed. No stronger digest or signature is generated in this task.

trace.description: The `package` Grunt task invokes the checksum task after creating the release archive; the task is run by a caller outside this file.
The checksum task enumerates all files in the distribution directory and reads each artifact for hashing.
Each artifact is hashed with the deprecated MD5 algorithm.
The resulting MD5 value is written as the artifact's verification file, making the weak digest the available release-integrity check.

title: Unauthenticated LLM tool can generate unrestricted discount coupons
description: The unauthenticated POST /rest/chat handler exposes the generateCoupon tool. Although the system prompt tells the model to enforce coupon eligibility and a 10% maximum, the tool implementation does not authenticate the requester, verify a damaged order, verify rejection of a return/exchange, or enforce the discount bound. The model can invoke security.generateCoupon with attacker-influenced tool arguments, allowing an unauthenticated caller to obtain coupons for arbitrary discount values, including values above the stated maximum.

trace.description: POST /rest/chat is registered without authentication or authorization middleware; the caller enters the chat handler in this file. The caller is outside this file, and the handler constructs tools for the request.

The generateCoupon tool accepts a caller-session-independent numeric discount and exposes an execution function. Its schema only checks that the value is a number; it does not enforce a maximum or bind the request to an authenticated customer or eligible order.

The chat request's messages are passed to the LLM together with the tool, so the model is given authority to decide when to invoke generateCoupon. The policy exists only in the system prompt and is not an independent authorization control.

The tool directly calls security.generateCoupon(discount) and returns the resulting coupon code without any server-side eligibility, ownership, authentication, or maximum-discount check. An unauthenticated attacker can prompt the model to invoke this path and receive the coupon.

title: User-controlled username is embedded into the LLM system prompt
description: The authenticated user's username is interpolated directly into the system prompt without fencing, escaping, or treating it as untrusted data. If a user can choose a username containing instruction-like text, that text is presented inside the system-instruction channel and can influence the model's behavior. In this handler, such prompt injection can be used to override the stated coupon policy or otherwise alter tool-selection behavior; the tool then performs actions based on the model's decision.

trace.description: POST /rest/chat receives attacker-controlled chat requests and resolves request-associated identity data. The caller and token contents originate outside this file.
The handler obtains the username associated with the request token and uses it as input to system-prompt construction; there is no visible validation or trust-boundary treatment for the username.

buildSystemPrompt concatenates userName into the system prompt as natural-language content, without delimiters or escaping that would prevent instruction-like username text from being interpreted as system instructions.

The resulting prompt is supplied as the model's system instruction while model-controlled tools, including generateCoupon, are enabled. Injected username text can therefore influence model decisions at a higher-priority prompt boundary.

title: Unauthenticated chat accepts unbounded message histories and LLM consumption
description: The chat endpoint accepts req.body.messages without a schema, maximum message count, maximum message length, or visible request-size limit, and passes the entire value to streamText. Because the route is unauthenticated and no rate-limit or per-request token budget is enforced in this file, an attacker can repeatedly submit very large conversation histories to consume LLM input tokens, memory, and provider capacity. The ten-step tool cap limits tool iterations but does not bound the initial prompt size or request frequency.

trace.description: POST /rest/chat is reachable without authentication or authorization middleware. The external caller enters this handler and can issue repeated requests.
The handler copies req.body.messages directly, defaulting only when the field is absent. No schema, message-count limit, per-message length limit, or body-size control is applied in this file.

The unbounded messages value is passed to streamText as the model conversation. Although stopWhen limits agent steps to 10, it does not cap input tokens or request frequency, and maxRetries may cause additional provider work.
streamText sends the attacker-supplied conversation to the configured LLM and streams the result, allowing oversized requests to consume application and upstream LLM resources.

title: Container base images are not pinned to immutable digests
description: Both container stages use mutable registry tags rather than immutable digests: `node:24` and `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13`. A rebuild can silently receive a different base image if the tag is retagged or the registry is compromised, changing the application’s runtime or build environment without a Dockerfile change. This weakens supply-chain integrity and makes incident investigation and reproducible deployment difficult.

trace.description: The Docker build receives the external build request and resolves the mutable `node:24` image tag declared for the installer stage.
The resulting application is transferred into a second image that also uses a mutable `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13` tag.
The mutable base-image tags are the security-relevant sink: any tag change affects the built artifact and can introduce altered or malicious build/runtime contents.

title: Build-time npm tooling is installed from mutable version ranges
description: The image build resolves global build tools from version ranges (`typescript@^6.0.3` and `@cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm@$CYCLONEDX_NPM_VERSION`, where the default is a set of ranges) on every build. These packages execute during the image build, and a newly published matching version or compromised package registry can execute code or alter the generated artifact. No immutable versions or integrity-pinned installation is shown for these global tools.

trace.description: An external Docker build triggers installation of the globally resolved TypeScript tool from the mutable `^6.0.3` range.
The build subsequently installs CycloneDX tooling using an ARG whose default contains multiple version ranges, so the selected package version can change between builds.
The unpinned global npm installations execute as build steps and are used to generate the SBOM, making dependency resolution a build-integrity sink.

title: Authenticated users can read arbitrary user records by ID
description: The authenticated GET /api/Users/:id endpoint performs only an authentication check and then exposes the generated Finale REST resource. There is no middleware here that scopes the requested id to the current user, so User A can substitute User B's numeric id and retrieve User B's record. This is a broken object-level authorization path.

trace.description: Entrypoint: GET /api/Users/:id receives the caller-controlled target user identifier in the :id path parameter.
The route applies security.isAuthorized(), which establishes authentication but does not visibly establish ownership or authorization for the selected user record.
Finale is configured to expose /api/Users/:id and performs the model lookup for the supplied id without an ownership constraint in this file.

title: Generated REST API permits mass assignment of model properties
description: The generated REST resources use exclude lists rather than explicit writable-field allow-lists. Most models have exclude: [], and the User resource excludes only password and totpSecret. Finale therefore automatically binds caller-supplied properties to model create/update operations. For User registration, an attacker can submit sensitive model properties such as a role/privilege flag if present in the model, potentially creating an elevated account; for other models, internal ownership, pricing, status, or permission fields may likewise become caller-controlled.

trace.description: The generated API exposes caller-facing CRUD endpoints for each model, including POST /api/Users and other model endpoints.

The resource configuration uses an exclude list, with empty lists for Product, Feedback, BasketItem, Complaint, Recycle, SecurityQuestion, SecurityAnswer, Address, PrivacyRequest, Card, Quantity, and Hint; User excludes only two fields rather than allowing only safe registration fields.
Finale creates the REST resource and automatically handles create/update binding for the configured Sequelize model, with no explicit property authorization or writable-field allow-list shown.

title: Unauthenticated FTP directory browsing and file download
description: Public FTP directory browsing and file serving are mounted without authentication or authorization middleware. An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate the FTP directory and download files placed there, including accidentally uploaded backups, credentials, or other internal artifacts.

trace.description: The application mounts the /ftp path as an externally reachable resource.

serveIndex('ftp', { icons: true }) enables directory enumeration, while the adjacent parameterized route exposes individual files; neither route is preceded by an authentication middleware in this file.
The /ftp/:file handler serves files from the FTP area to the caller.

title: Memory upload endpoint allows unbounded disk consumption
description: The /rest/memories upload endpoint uses multer disk storage without a fileSize or other body-size limit. A caller can submit a valid image MIME type with an arbitrarily large payload; multer writes it to the server's upload directory before the application handler runs. Repeated uploads can exhaust disk space and degrade or stop service.

trace.description: Entrypoint: POST /rest/memories accepts a caller-supplied multipart file and invokes uploadToDisk.single('image').
The disk-backed multer instance defines MIME-based naming and destination handling but supplies no limits option, unlike the separately configured memory uploader.
Valid uploads are written to the application upload directory, with no size cap before disk persistence.

title: Generated collection endpoints disable pagination
description: All generated Finale resources are configured with pagination: false. Public or broadly accessible list endpoints such as product and challenge collections can therefore return the entire table in one request. As data grows, a single request can force unbounded database, application-memory, serialization, and network work, enabling denial of service.

trace.description: The generated REST API creates collection endpoints such as /api/Products and /api/Challenges, which can be reached through the configured application routes.
Each generated resource explicitly disables pagination, so collection requests have no application-level result-size bound.
Finale serves the resulting unbounded model collections through its automatic REST handlers.

title: Hardcoded weak cookie-signing secret
description: The application enables signed cookie parsing with the literal secret 'kekse' embedded in source. Anyone who obtains or guesses this weak secret can forge signatures for cookies processed by cookie-parser. Even if the currently visible language cookie is the primary use, a hardcoded signing secret is unsafe and can become security-impacting if signed cookies are later used for trust decisions.

trace.description: The application initialization path configures cookie parsing for all subsequent requests.
cookie-parser is initialized with the source-code literal 'kekse' as its signing secret rather than a deployment secret.
Signed-cookie verification and signature generation use this hardcoded secret, allowing forgery when the value is known.

title: Password-reset rate limiting is bypassable through forwarded IP identity
description: The server globally enables Express trust proxy and then uses the client-forwarded address as the reset-password rate-limit identity. In deployments where the application is directly reachable or the proxy does not sanitize X-Forwarded-For, an attacker can rotate the forwarded value and evade the 100-request window. This permits high-volume password-reset attempts and account-recovery abuse.

trace.description: The password-reset route applies a rate limiter intended to constrain account-recovery requests.
The application trusts proxy-derived client IP information globally, and the limiter's custom key generator derives its key from X-Forwarded-For or req.ip.
The limiter enforces the request window using that caller-influenced identity, allowing forwarded-IP rotation to bypass throttling when upstream sanitization is absent.
